(* --- self-wiring prologue ---------------------------------------------------- Makes the InitMqtt and InitMqttDiscovery* calls optional. Set FriendlyName at the declaration site and this block wires itself from GVL_MQTT on its first cyclic call, then announces itself to Home Assistant.

documentation.xhtml: Degrees Celsius. Held at the last trustworthy reading while Fault is set, rather than following the channel into whatever it reports for a broken wire.
The channel is reading a real sensor, within what the sensor type can measure AND within what this sensor could plausibly be measuring.

Do not trust this reading. Set when the value is outside what the sensor type can physically produce, and when the channel has gone StaleTimeout without moving a digit, and when it is outside PlausibleMin..PlausibleMax. This is what drives the entity's availability: while it is set, Home Assistant shows the sensor as unavailable.

High once a plausible reading has been seen, and it latches. It answers "has this channel ever worked", not "is it working now" - Valid is that one.
One wart, found by a bench assertion that expected better: a mapped channel reads 0 for the first cycles, before the K-bus has filled the process image, and 0.0 C is a perfectly plausible reading. So this latches TRUE - and Temperature holds 0.0 - even on a channel that goes on to measure nothing at all. Do not read it as proof a sensor is connected.
object's full instance name
FALSE only in the moments after the bus comes up, while the channel still reads the zero the process image was cleared to.

The channel word as it was last published, so a repeat can be told from a change. Kept as the INT rather than the REAL: two readings that came from the same word are then equal by construction, with no float comparison.
LeadResistance expressed in the module's own units - tenths of a degree.
Raw with the lead correction taken off. Everything downstream reads this rather than Raw, except the movement check.

What a platinum RTD can physically report, per IEC 60751: -200 C to 850 C. Anything outside it is the module telling you about the wiring rather than the temperature, whatever value it happens to use to say so - which is why the check is a range in engineering units and not a magic fault code.

How long a channel may read exactly 0 after the bus comes up before 0 is believed as a temperature.
ProcessImageValid is necessary and NOT sufficient: the bus reports process data exchanging a little before an RTD module has delivered its first conversion, and in that window the word is still the zeroed process image. Measured on the bench, that window is well under a second - but 0 is 0.0 C, a perfectly plausible temperature, so a block that believes it publishes a fabricated zero on every restart.
Long enough for any 750-series RTD to convert, short enough that a sensor genuinely sitting at 0.0 C is only briefly unavailable rather than wrong.

dR/dT of a Pt1000 near room temperature, per IEC 60751. The local slope at 0 C is 3.9083; 3.85 is the mean coefficient over 0..100 C and is the wrong number here, because a lead correction is applied where the sensor is, not averaged over its whole span.

The mapped channel word of an RTD input module, in tenths of a degree Celsius - which is what a WAGO 750-463 and its relatives put in the process image, two's complement, so -105 is -10.5 C. Wire it straight to the channel variable: Raw := RTD_001.

TRUE once the K-bus has finished starting and is really exchanging process data. Until then every mapped word reads 0, and 0 is 0.0 C - a perfectly plausible temperature - so a block that trusts it publishes a fabricated zero on every restart before the real value arrives a second later. That happened, on this bench, and it is why this input exists.
Wire it to the bus driver's own answer, which is the only authoritative one: ProcessImageValid := Pfc200Bus.xConfigFinished.
Defaults to FALSE, deliberately. Forget to wire it and the channel stays unavailable, which is loud; the alternative default hands you a wrong number once per restart, which is silent.

Round-trip resistance of the sensor leads, in ohms. Zero, and nothing is corrected.
A 750-451 and a 750-463 both measure 2-conductor, so nothing compensates for the wire: the leads sit in series with the element and the channel reads HIGH by them. Near room temperature a Pt1000 moves about 3.9 ohms per degree, so the error is LeadResistance / 3.9 degrees - about 0.18 C down 2x10 m of 0.5 mm2, and 1.8 C down 2x50 m of 0.25 mm2. Ignorable on a bench, not ignorable on a long run.
Measure it with the sensor disconnected, by shorting the far end of the pair and reading the loop at the terminals.
CORRECT THIS IN ONE PLACE ONLY. The module carries its own user scaling and user calibration, written with WAGO-I/O-CHECK and unreadable from CODESYS - set an offset there as well and it is applied twice, with nothing anywhere to say so. Prefer here: this is in source control, it shows up in a diff and in the PLCopen export, and it survives swapping the terminal, which a value in a module's flash does not.

Republish even when nothing changed, so a reader can tell a steady temperature from a PLC that has stopped. Paired with the discovery config's expire_after, which is set to three of these - so a minute here means Home Assistant gives up on a silent channel after three.

The range this sensor could plausibly be measuring, in degrees Celsius.
The IEC 60751 bounds only ask whether a platinum RTD could produce a reading at all, which turns out to be a very weak question: a WAGO 750-463 reports an open circuit as 150.0 C, a legal Pt1000 temperature that passes the range check and publishes as healthy until StaleTimeout eventually notices. No room, buffer tank or floor loop reaches 150 C, so saying what this sensor is for rejects that on the first scan instead of a quarter of an hour later.
Widen it deliberately for a flue, a solar collector or a freezer. Set Max <= Min to switch the check off.
Pointer to the discovery device this entity belongs to, normally GVL_MQTT.PLC_Device. An RTD channel is part of the PLC rather than a device of its own.
Name of the entity in Home Assistant. The self-wiring prologue passes FriendlyName.
Overrides the generated entity id. Leave empty to derive it from the function block name.
Extra JSON merged into the discovery config. Rarely needed.
Publishes the Home Assistant MQTT discovery configs - a temperature sensor and a diagnostic fault flag - so both entities are created automatically. Call once at startup, after InitMqtt.

A single-producer / single-consumer ring buffer.
EMPTY and FULL used to be stored BOOL outputs, written by both sides, and that was the whole problem. With iPw = iPr the ring is either completely empty or completely full, and only those two flags told the cases apart - so a task that lost a race on them could leave a non-empty queue looking empty (the workers stop draining, and a retained state change sits unsent until the next publish), or clear FULL while the ring really was full (a writer then overruns entries the reader has not taken yet).
They are derived now. HasMessage() is iPr <> iPw; IsFull() is INC1(iPw,ciN) = iPr. Nothing shared is mutable any more: iPw is written only by AddMessage, iPr only by GetMessage, and each side merely reads the other's index - a single aligned INT load on this 32-bit target, which cannot tear. No semaphore, so no priority inversion on MainTask or HvacTask.
The cost is exactly one slot. Reporting full one slot early is what buys iPw = iPr its unambiguous "empty" meaning, so capacity is ciN rather than ciN+1.
What this does NOT fix: two tasks inside AddMessage at the same time can still read the same iPw, leave one hybrid message in that slot and the next slot never written at all. Only one queue per producer fixes that.

Arbitrates one RS485 bus between the aitfDevices registered on it.
The unit of arbitration is a TRANSACTION: an ordered list of eSteps that a device hands over in one go, executed back to back with the bus held throughout. That is what makes a write and its read-back inseparable - no other device's traffic can land between them - and it is why a meter with three register blocks now wins the bus once per poll round instead of three times.
Selection resumes at a cursor rather than restarting at device 0, so the device registered last is served as often as the device registered first. The old loop ran FOR 0 TO count-1 and took the first taker, which is strict priority by registration order dressed up as a scan.
Commands are looked for before polls, each pass round-robin from the same cursor, so a Home Assistant command does not queue behind every meter while a chatty device still cannot starve a quiet one.
The protocol lives behind I_RS485_TRANSPORT. This block never sees a CRC, a function code or a serial handle.

ST.xhtml:
(* Round-robin from the cursor, twice: once for work somebody is waiting on, once for routine polling.
Starting each pass at Cursor rather than at 0 is the whole fairness story. The loop this replaces ran FOR 0 TO iDevicesCount - 1 and EXITed on the first taker, so device 0 won every contested cycle and the device registered last only ever got the bus when everything above it was idle. With two meters on five-second polls that is invisible; with thirty nodes it is starvation.
Both passes sweep every device, so a COMMAND anywhere beats a POLL everywhere - but COMMANDs are themselves served round-robin, so a chatty device cannot monopolise the bus either. *)
SelectNext := -1;
FOR iK := 0 TO iDevicesCount - 1 DO iI := (Cursor + iK) MOD iDevicesCount; IF aitfDevices[iI].HasWork() = E_RS485_WORK_LEVEL.COMMAND THEN SelectNext := iI; RETURN; END_IF END_FOR
FOR iK := 0 TO iDevicesCount - 1 DO iI := (Cursor + iK) MOD iDevicesCount; IF aitfDevices[iI].HasWork() = E_RS485_WORK_LEVEL.POLL THEN SelectNext := iI; RETURN; END_IF END_FOR

Availability is a judgement, not a reading. One missed reply on a shared RS485 bus is ordinary - a slave that was mid-measurement, a collision with another device's turnaround - and publishing 'offline' on the strength of it makes the Home Assistant connectivity sensor flap between states that are both wrong. So failures have to accumulate before the device is declared down, and recovery is immediate on the first good transaction: being slow to trust and quick to forgive is the right asymmetry when the cost of a false 'offline' is an entity that looks broken.

Quality, which is a different question from availability and needs a different answer. Availability is binary and has to be debounced or it reports noise; that same debounce means a sensor answering two polls in three still reads 'online', which is true and useless. This is the signal that says how well it is working rather than whether it is: the share of the last sixteen transactions that succeeded, as a percentage. A sensor degrading - a loose pair, a failing driver, a bus getting busier - shows up here long before it shows up as a disconnection.

This is the code that was proven on the bench in #182, lifted out of the RS485_RUN action into a block of its own and taught the write function codes it was missing. Two things about this hardware are baked in and deliberate:
- Every reply arrives wrapped in glitch bytes - one 00 as the slave's driver enables, another as it releases, because the pair is undriven between frames. Measured across 34 consecutive captures: 34 leading nulls, 34 trailing nulls, 34 wCrc-bDataValid frames once trimmed. So the frame is trimmed and the wCrc judges what is left, rather than the iFirst byte being trusted.
- The frame is delimited by silence, which is what RTU actually specifies, not by a byte count read out of the header.

(* Find the frame inside what has been collected. Sets `iFirst` and `iLast`, and returns whether the bytes between them check out.
Counts nothing, changes no iState beyond those two indices, and is safe to call every cycle - which is the point. Service uses it to notice that a frame is already complete instead of waiting out the silence, and Judge uses it to decide what it is looking at.
This RESYNCHRONISES rather than merely trimming a leading run of nulls, and that distinction is the whole reason it was rewritten. Trimming nulls handles the driver-enable glitch this hardware produces, and nothing else: put any non-zero byte in front of the reply and every wCrc trial fails, because the window always started at that byte. Measured on a DFRobot SEN0492, one reply in three was being thrown away that way - bytes present, LeadNulls climbing, CrcFail climbing, and the sensor answering perfectly well the whole time.
Three things put a non-zero byte in front of a reply, and all of them are ordinary rather than exotic: - a slave that echoes the request before answering, which is documented behaviour for the SEN0492 and reported for others; - a byte left over from the previous exchange that arrived after Start flushed the port; - two replies collected into one window, when a slave answers late enough to land inside the next poll. All three are cured by asking "does a valid frame start HERE?" at every plausible offset instead of assuming the answer is offset zero.
The search is anchored on the slave address rather than sweeping blindly, which keeps the number of wCrc trials small and, more importantly, keeps the chance of a coincidental wCrc match negligible. *) Frame := FALSE; iFirst := 0;

(* Trailing bytes are removed by asking the wCrc rather than by assuming a trailing 00 is noise. It usually is - but a frame whose wCrc high byte is genuinely 00 turns up about once in 256, and blindly trimming it turned a perfectly good reply into a wCrc failure. *) iLast := count; iTries := 0;

END_WHILE
